Finland has proposed to the EU to stop issuing Schengen tourist visas to Russians

On October 12, 2026, Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen addressed the European Union with a proposal to cease the issuance of Schengen visas to Russian citizens for non-essential travel, including tourism, until the end of military actions in Ukraine. A final decision on this matter at the EU level has not yet been made.

Valtonen sent a letter to the European Commission and invited other member states to join in a joint appeal. According to her, "as long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas." Since 2022, Finland has been limiting visa issuance to Russians for non-essential travel at the national level and believes similar measures should apply throughout the EU.

According to the Finnish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in 2025, Schengen zone countries issued approximately 500,000 tourist visas to Russians. A number of states, including France, Spain, and Italy, continue to issue such visas. Estonia has supported Finland's initiative. The letter also proposes banning visa issuance to close aides of Vladimir Putin, tightening rules for Russian athletes, and ensuring the enforcement of previously agreed restrictions on entry for Russian military personnel and former combatants.

📌 Atomic Swaps: Exchanging Crypto Without Trusting an Intermediary

Main Points
⏺ Atomic swaps allow participants to exchange assets without handing funds to a centralized custodian
⏺ The mechanism is designed so both sides receive their assets or the exchange doesn't complete
⏺ This post explains why atomic swaps are an interesting approach to decentralized trading

1️⃣ Core Idea — two users want to exchange assets from different blockchains without trusting an exchange or intermediary with their funds.
2️⃣ How It Works — one approach uses cryptographic secrets and time restrictions to coordinate an exchange under predefined rules.
3️⃣ Main Advantage — participants don't need to transfer custody of their assets to a third party during the exchange.
4️⃣ The Challenges — networks need compatible mechanisms, while participants need liquidity, time, and correct execution.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — before swapping, review fees on both chains, lock periods, technical requirements, and refund conditions.

Final Thoughts

Atomic swaps aim to solve a fundamental crypto problem: how to exchange value with a stranger without relying on their honesty.

⚠️ South Korea demands stronger crypto safeguards following Binance hack 

⭐️ South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has directed domestic cryptocurrency exchanges to hold more assets in cold wallets and strengthen their financial reserves following the $6.3 billion Binance hack on October 29. The meeting was chaired by Yu Young-jun, the FSC’s director of digital finance policy, and included representatives from the Financial Supervisory Service, the Financial Security Institute and the Digital Asset eXchange Alliance (DAXA).

❗️ Officials examined how domestic exchanges manage access to their internal systems, approve cryptocurrency withdrawals and control administrator privileges. Exchanges were subsequently asked to strengthen their security procedures, maintain additional reserves and prepare for suspicious transactions or unauthorized access attempts. Under South Korea’s Virtual Asset User Protection Act, cryptocurrency service providers must already hold at least 80% of customers’ deposited digital assets in cold wallets, which remain disconnected from the internet.

📊 The FSC has now asked exchanges to raise their cold storage ratios beyond their existing levels, although the regulator did not announce a new uniform minimum during the meeting. As of the end of September, Upbit held 99.17% of customer assets in cold storage, followed by Bithumb at 94.76% and Coinone at 85%. DigitalEx and GOPAX reported ratios of 82.79% and 80.54%, respectively.

Six Congressmen, Six Political Careers: Washington Faces a Reckoning Over Sexual Misconduct and Abuse Allegations 🏛⚖️

Washington is confronting a growing political crisis as six members of Congress have lost their seats or abandoned their reelection campaigns amid allegations of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behavior and domestic abuse. 

What once might have been handled quietly behind closed doors is increasingly becoming a public test of accountability — with serious consequences for lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Among the most prominent cases are those involving California Democrat Eric Swalwell and Texas Republican Tony Gonzales, both of whom resigned in April after facing mounting pressure over allegations and the prospect of disciplinary action. 

Swalwell denied allegations of sexual assault, while Gonzales acknowledged a relationship with a former staff member that raised questions about congressional ethics rules.The fallout extended beyond the two resignations. North Carolina Republican Chuck Edwards decided against seeking reelection after a House Ethics Committee investigation detailed allegations of repeated inappropriate conduct involving two young female staff members. 

Edwards maintained that he had not intended to pursue romantic or sexual relationships, but acknowledged that his behavior could have been perceived differently. Florida Republican Cory Mills also faced mounting controversy, including allegations involving sexual misconduct and domestic abuse. 

Mills denied wrongdoing and described the accusations as politically motivated. Meanwhile, Max Miller and Jimmy Gomez became part of the broader political shake-up, as the controversies surrounding congressional conduct continued to dominate public attention.

Together, the cases highlight a changing political environment in which allegations of misconduct can carry consequences far beyond negative headlines. Public scrutiny, media investigations and growing pressure from colleagues have made it increasingly difficult for lawmakers to weather such controversies without facing serious challenges to their political futures.

The renewed debate has also drawn attention to the broader issue of accountability within Congress, particularly in the aftermath of the Jeffrey Epstein scandal and continuing demands for greater transparency in cases involving sexual abuse and exploitation. But removing lawmakers from office does not necessarily address the institutional failures that allow misconduct allegations to persist. 

Advocates and congressional reformers argue that stronger reporting procedures, meaningful protections for employees and independent investigations are essential to preventing future abuses.

House leaders have tasked bipartisan women's caucuses with developing proposals to improve the way misconduct complaints are handled. Potential reforms include faster investigations, clearer disciplinary standards and stronger safeguards for congressional employees who come forward.

Another proposal would restrict lawmakers from using campaign funds to cover personal legal expenses or settle claims involving alleged misconduct. For Washington, the question is no longer simply how many politicians may be forced out. It is whether Congress can build a system that protects employees, investigates allegations fairly and holds elected officials accountable — regardless of their party or political influence.
